title: Local assistant — component harvest
subtitle: Ranked open-source candidates for each part the project has to build.
target_stack: Rust · desktop shell · local inference · Apple Silicon, local-first

components.title: Crew orchestration & rounds
components.job: Run a five-role crew in turns, with work able to travel backwards between rounds.

ranked.why: Cyclic state graphs with checkpointing and human-in-the-loop pause/resume — the closest existing match to rounds that can send work back.
ranked.promote: Stays first unless the crew turns out to need role personas more than explicit flow control.
ranked.fit: Python. Sits beside the brain, not inside the Tauri core.

ranked.why: Far larger community and role-based crews out of the box, but flow control is implicit — sending work backwards means fighting the abstraction.
ranked.promote: Promote if you want personas and delegation for free and can live without an explicit state machine.
ranked.fit: Python. Same placement as LangGraph.

ranked.why: Fast and light, with much lower startup cost per agent — but fewer durable-state primitives, so a crashed round is harder to resume.
ranked.promote: Promote if agent spin-up latency becomes the bottleneck and rounds stay short.
ranked.fit: Python. Good if the queue restarts agents often.

ranked.why: Excellent typed tool-calling and structured output, but it is not a crew framework — you would build the rounds yourself.
ranked.promote: Promote if the real need turns out to be reliable structured tool calls rather than orchestration.
ranked.fit: Python. Would pair with a hand-written scheduler.

ranked.why: Large and well known, but momentum slowed (last push April) and it carries CC-BY-4.0, a content licence that is an odd fit for shipped code.
ranked.promote: Promote only if a specific conversation pattern here is otherwise unavailable — and read the licence first.
ranked.fit: Python. Licence needs legal review before shipping.

excluded.name: openai/swarm
excluded.why: Experimental and superseded by OpenAI's agents SDK; last push April 2026.

components.title: Durable task queue
components.job: One global queue across projects, ordered by position, urgency and priority, surviving a 3am reboot.

ranked.why: Built for agent workloads specifically: durable step-level state, automatic retries and live stream telemetry — which is what the cockpit's progress view needs.
ranked.promote: Stays first unless you decide the queue must live in-process rather than as a service.
ranked.fit: Go service + Python/TS clients. Runs alongside the brain.

ranked.why: The most battle-tested durable execution engine here, but it is a cluster — heavy for a single laptop that also has to run two models.
ranked.promote: Promote if the queue ever spans more than one machine.
ranked.fit: Go. Meaningful resource cost on a shared laptop.

ranked.why: The best architectural fit — native Rust, embeds directly in the Tauri process, no extra service. Smallest ecosystem of the five, so more will be hand-built.
ranked.promote: Promote if you want zero extra processes and are willing to write the retry and priority logic yourself.
ranked.fit: Rust. Lives inside the Tauri core.

ranked.why: Clean and reliable, but Postgres-only — which means running Postgres purely to hold a local queue.
ranked.promote: Promote if Postgres is already a hard dependency for other reasons.
ranked.fit: Go + Postgres. Adds a database to the local stack.

ranked.why: Durable workflows as plain Python decorators, very low ceremony — but young, and the smallest community here.
ranked.promote: Promote if the brain stays Python-centric and the queue never needs to be reached from Rust.
ranked.fit: Python. Would sit in the brain process.

components.title: Execution sandbox
components.job: Run untrusted package installs and third-party code without reaching the rest of the machine.

ranked.why: Apple's own tool, running Linux containers as lightweight VMs on Apple Silicon — a real kernel boundary, native to the target platform, no third-party runtime.
ranked.promote: Stays first for anything needing a strong boundary on this hardware.
ranked.fit: Swift, macOS 26+, Apple Silicon. Native fit.

ranked.why: Mature and scriptable Linux VMs on macOS, more configurable than Apple's tool — but a heavier install and slower to start.
ranked.promote: Promote if you need fine control over the VM, or support for macOS versions Apple's container does not cover.
ranked.fit: Go. Works on Apple Silicon, extra install.

ranked.why: Docker-compatible on macOS with almost no setup, so existing container tooling just works.
ranked.promote: Promote if the project ends up needing Docker CLI compatibility specifically.
ranked.fit: Go, wraps Lima. Extra install.

ranked.why: Purpose-built for AI agent code execution with excellent streaming APIs — but it is a hosted service, so code and files leave the machine.
ranked.promote: Promote only for a project explicitly allowed to use cloud execution.
ranked.fit: Hosted microVMs. Conflicts with local-first unless self-hosted.

ranked.why: The microVM technology underneath most agent sandboxes, and written in Rust — but it needs Linux and KVM, so it cannot run directly on macOS.
ranked.promote: Promote if the project ever runs on a Linux host.
ranked.fit: Rust, Linux/KVM only. Not runnable on this Mac.

ranked.why: Strong syscall-level isolation, but Linux-only and operationally complex.
ranked.promote: Promote only on a Linux deployment with a hard multi-tenant requirement.
ranked.fit: Go, Linux only.

excluded.name: containers/bubblewrap
excluded.why: Linux namespaces — cannot run on macOS at all. It was the previous dashboard's recommendation for this component.

excluded.name: macOS Seatbelt (sandbox-exec)
excluded.why: Not a repository: it ships with macOS. Still the cheapest real boundary for a local process, and the intended floor here.

components.title: Guardrails & admission control
components.job: Constrain what a model may do, and refuse requests that fall outside policy.

ranked.why: Programmable rails with a dedicated policy language, and the most complete dialogue-level controls — but GitHub detects no licence file, which needs resolving before shipping.
ranked.promote: Stays first if the licence checks out; drops immediately if it does not.
ranked.fit: Python. Licence unresolved — verify before adopting.

ranked.why: Clear Apache-2.0 licence and good output validators, but weaker at conversation-level policy than NeMo.
ranked.promote: Promote the moment licence certainty matters more than policy depth — which for a project going public, it probably does.
ranked.fit: Python. Clean licence, safe default.

ranked.why: Not a rails engine at all — it detects and redacts personal data, which is the other half of the admission problem and the only candidate here that serves the screen-capture redaction requirement directly.
ranked.promote: Promote to first if the real risk turns out to be personal data leaving in a payload rather than a model doing something it should not.
ranked.fit: Python, MIT, clean licence. Note it moved from `microsoft/presidio`.

ranked.why: A vulnerability scanner rather than a guard: it finds the holes instead of closing them, so it complements the rails above rather than replacing them.
ranked.promote: Use alongside whichever rails ship, to test that they actually hold.
ranked.fit: Python, Apache-2.0. Testing tool, not a runtime dependency.

excluded.name: protectai/llm-guard
excluded.why: ARCHIVED. Looks healthy at a glance — 3.2k stars, pushed July 2026 — but the repository is archived and will not receive fixes.

components.title: Skills library & tool registry
components.job: A library of skill files and tools that agents invoke at run time.

ranked.why: Matches the Tauri core's language, so tool registration lives in the same process as the bridge. Smallest of the SDKs, and GitHub detects no licence file.
ranked.promote: Stays first for anything registered inside the Rust core; check the licence before shipping.
ranked.fit: Rust. Native fit for the Tauri side.

ranked.why: The most complete SDK with a clear MIT licence, and the brain is already Python — but it puts tool hosting in the brain rather than the core.
ranked.promote: Promote if tools should live with the brain instead of the shell.
ranked.fit: Python. Fits the existing brain process.

ranked.why: The reference server collection — the fastest way to get working tools — but it is examples rather than a library, and no licence is detected at repo level.
ranked.promote: Promote as a source of implementations to read, not as a dependency.
ranked.fit: TypeScript/Python. Reference material.

ranked.why: The largest directory of available servers, invaluable for discovery — but it is a list, not code.
ranked.promote: Never promotes to a dependency; use it to find candidates.
ranked.fit: Directory. Discovery only.

ranked.why: A complete Rust agent with an extension system worth reading closely — and it moved: `block/goose` now redirects here.
ranked.promote: Promote if you want a whole extension architecture to adapt rather than a protocol SDK.
ranked.fit: Rust, Apache-2.0. Note the org rename.

components.title: Wake word detection
components.job: Detect the summon word locally, with no audio leaving the machine until it fires.

ranked.why: Fully open, trains custom wake words, runs entirely offline with no key or service — the only candidate that meets the local-first requirement outright.
ranked.promote: Stays first unless detection accuracy proves unusable in practice.
ranked.fit: Python/ONNX. Runs local; needs a Rust or Swift binding for the shell.

ranked.why: The best accuracy and the lowest CPU cost by a distance, with real Apple Silicon support — but the models are commercially licensed and gated behind an access key, which conflicts with shipping an open project.
ranked.promote: Promote if accuracy turns out to matter more than licence purity, and only for personal use.
ranked.fit: Multi-platform. Licence conflicts with an open release.

ranked.why: Offline recognition with keyword spotting, so one engine could cover both the summon word and dictation — heavier than a dedicated detector, and it has to stay resident to listen.
ranked.promote: Promote if running one always-on engine beats running a detector plus a separate transcriber.
ranked.fit: C++/Python bindings, Apache-2.0. Runs local; heavier idle cost.

ranked.why: A service wrapper around openWakeWord with a clean protocol, which removes the binding work — but it is small, and adds a process to supervise.
ranked.promote: Promote if you would rather speak to a local service than embed a Python model in the shell.
ranked.fit: Python, Apache-2.0. Adds a supervised process.

excluded.name: MycroftAI/mycroft-precise
excluded.why: Last pushed November 2023 — effectively abandoned, and the parent project shut down.

excluded.name: kahrendt/microWakeWord
excluded.why: The slug resolves to a 4-star repository, which does not match the known project — treat as unverified and search again before considering it.

excluded.name: Kitt-AI/snowboy
excluded.why: Last pushed October 2021 and the company shut down; the hosted training service it depended on is gone.

components.title: Screen & GUI understanding
components.job: Answer "what am I looking at", and learn from a video he is watching.

ranked.why: Continuous screen capture with local search and indexing, written in Rust and built for macOS — the closest thing to the requirement, and it moved from `mediar-ai/screenpipe`.
ranked.promote: Stays first for the always-available screen context; no licence detected, so verify before shipping.
ranked.fit: Rust, macOS-native. Licence unresolved.

ranked.why: Turns a screenshot into structured UI elements, which is what makes a VLM's answer about a screen precise rather than vague — but CC-BY-4.0 is a content licence and needs review.
ranked.promote: Promote when the task shifts from 'describe my screen' to 'act on my screen'.
ranked.fit: Python model. Licence needs review.

ranked.why: Records screen, mouse and keyboard together to learn workflows — closest to 'watch me and help me do that', but much smaller and less mature.
ranked.promote: Promote if demonstration-by-example becomes a real feature rather than a curiosity.
ranked.fit: Python, MIT. Smallest community here.

ranked.why: By far the most active project in this set, and excellent — but it drives a browser, not the screen, so it answers a narrower question than the one asked.
ranked.promote: Promote for anything specifically about web pages rather than the whole desktop.
ranked.fit: Python, MIT. Browser only.

components.title: State snapshotting & history
components.job: A hidden version history from the first file written, so any overnight decision can be undone.

ranked.why: A pure-Rust git implementation that embeds directly in the Tauri core — no shelling out, no git binary dependency, and it moved from `Byron/gitoxide`.
ranked.promote: Stays first for history written from inside the app.
ranked.fit: Rust, Apache-2.0. Native fit.

ranked.why: Snapshots the working copy automatically without anyone writing commit logic — arguably a better conceptual match for an invisible safety history than git itself.
ranked.promote: Promote if automatic snapshots matter more than embedding, and running a binary is acceptable.
ranked.fit: Rust binary, Apache-2.0. Invoked, not embedded.

ranked.why: The most mature and complete git library anywhere, but it is C — FFI, and no licence detected at repo level (it is GPL-2.0 with a linking exception, which needs reading).
ranked.promote: Promote if gitoxide turns out to be missing an operation you need.
ranked.fit: C. FFI plus a licence to read carefully.

ranked.why: Pure JavaScript git, already patched and in use in this project's dependency tree — but it belongs to the front end, not the core.
ranked.promote: Promote for anything the web layer must do without the Rust side.
ranked.fit: JavaScript, MIT. Already present in the repo.

ranked.why: Excellent deduplicating backups, but a backup is not a history — it cannot answer "undo the decision made at 3am".
ranked.promote: Promote for protecting the projects folder as a whole, alongside a real history rather than instead of one.
ranked.fit: Go binary. Complementary, not a substitute.

components.title: Roadmap & Kanban UI
components.job: A cockpit with a roadmap and to-do lists, at project level and across all projects.

ranked.why: The drag-and-drop primitive for React, accessible and unopinionated — you build the cockpit you designed rather than adopting someone else's board.
ranked.promote: Stays first while the cockpit is a bespoke surface.
ranked.fit: TypeScript/React, MIT. Drops into the existing shell.

ranked.why: Framework-agnostic and extremely widely used, with a simpler mental model — but an older imperative API that fits React less naturally.
ranked.promote: Promote if dnd-kit's abstractions get in the way.
ranked.fit: JavaScript, MIT. Works anywhere.

ranked.why: A complete project management product with cycles, modules and roadmaps — a rich source of interaction ideas, but AGPL-3.0, which would force the licence of anything it is linked into.
ranked.promote: Promote only as a reference to study, never as an embedded dependency.
ranked.fit: TypeScript, AGPL-3.0. Licence blocks embedding.

ranked.why: Beautiful local-first workspace with kanban and boards, and a Rust core — but it is Flutter and also AGPL-3.0.
ranked.promote: Promote as a design reference for local-first boards; the licence rules it out as a dependency.
ranked.fit: Dart/Flutter + Rust, AGPL-3.0. Reference only.

components.title: Presence detection
components.job: Open the mic when he is at the machine, and close it when he is not — without using the camera.

ranked.why: A small, readable implementation of the IOPMAssertion pattern — the exact API for keeping the machine awake and observing power state.
ranked.promote: Reference implementation rather than a dependency; stays first as the thing to read.
ranked.fit: Objective-C, MIT. Read it, do not link it.

ranked.why: Reliable active-window and focus detection on macOS, which is a decent proxy for presence; it moved from `sindresorhus/active-win`.
ranked.promote: Promote if window focus turns out to be a better presence signal than input idle time.
ranked.fit: JavaScript/Swift helper, MIT. Note the rename.

ranked.why: A break reminder whose idle-detection logic is worth reading, since it solves the same 'is the human here' problem.
ranked.promote: Reference only.
ranked.fit: JavaScript, BSD-2. Read the idle logic.

excluded.name: IOKit HIDIdleTime
excluded.why: Not a repository: the system API these projects all wrap. Reading idle time and lock state directly needs no dependency at all, which is very likely the right answer here.

components.title: Speech to text
components.job: Transcribe him locally, in Hebrew and English, fast enough to feel like conversation.

ranked.why: WhisperKit's home after the rename — CoreML and Apple Neural Engine inference, the fastest path on this exact hardware, in Swift.
ranked.promote: Stays first while the target is Apple Silicon only.
ranked.fit: Swift, MIT. Best Apple Silicon fit; note the rename from `argmaxinc/WhisperKit`.

ranked.why: The most portable and most used, with Metal acceleration and an enormous ecosystem — slightly slower than CoreML on this hardware but far easier to embed anywhere.
ranked.promote: Promote the moment the project needs to run on anything that is not an Apple Silicon Mac.
ranked.fit: C++, MIT. Metal on Apple Silicon.

ranked.why: Built for short utterances and noticeably faster than Whisper on them, which suits a wake-word-triggered assistant — but no licence is detected and it moved from `usefulsensors/moonshine`.
ranked.promote: Promote if latency on short commands becomes the complaint; resolve the licence first.
ranked.fit: C++/Python. Licence unresolved.

ranked.why: Strong CTranslate2 implementation, but oriented to CUDA — the advantage largely disappears on Apple Silicon.
ranked.promote: Promote only if inference moves to an NVIDIA machine.
ranked.fit: Python. Weaker fit on this hardware.

components.title: Push relay & mobile sync
components.job: Reach his phone when he is away, with the relay self-hosted rather than a service he depends on.

ranked.why: Self-hosted push with published iOS and Android apps and a trivial HTTP API — the only candidate that satisfies "every user runs their own relay" without building a phone app first.
ranked.promote: Stays first unless the phone experience needs to be a full custom app rather than notifications.
ranked.fit: Go, Apache-2.0. Self-hosted, apps exist.

ranked.why: A fast Nostr relay in C++, matching the sync protocol this project already speaks — but Nostr relays carry events, not push notifications, so it complements ntfy rather than replacing it.
ranked.promote: Promote if phone sync should ride the existing Nostr transport instead of a second channel.
ranked.fit: C++, GPL-3.0. GPL needs consideration for a shipped bundle.

ranked.why: The specification the existing relay implements — essential reading for anything touching sync, but not an implementation.
ranked.promote: Never promotes to a dependency.
ranked.fit: Specification. Reference material.

excluded.name: fiatjaf/khatru
excluded.why: ARCHIVED. A well-regarded Go relay framework, but archived in September 2025 — it would have looked like a reasonable pick from memory.
